title: Variables and Data Types
learning_objective: Store a single value in a variable with the correct data type (str, int, float, bool) and predict the type Python assigns to a given value.
description_for_ai: A variable is created with a single equals sign, e.g. branch_name = "Lagos", and holds one value until reassigned. Python infers the type automatically from the value: text wrapped in quotation marks is str, whole numbers are int, numbers with a decimal point are float, and True/False, capitalised and unquoted, is bool. type(variable_name) reveals the actual type Python assigned. A value only becomes a string because of the quotation marks around it, not because of what it looks like, so "145000" is a str even though it reads like a number, while 145000 without quotes is an int.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Believing a numeric-looking string such as "145000" is automatically treated as a number because it is written using digits. Forgetting quotation marks around text, which raises a NameError because Python tries to interpret the words as variable names instead of a string literal. Assuming True and False need quotation marks like other words, when they must be written unquoted and capitalised to be recognised as the bool type. Confusing int and float, expecting 15000 and 15000.0 to be treated identically in all contexts.
example_code_for_ai:
branch_name = "Lagos"
total_sales = 245000
average_sale = 15312.50
target_met = True

print(type(branch_name))
print(type(total_sales))
print(type(average_sale))
print(type(target_met))

title: Lists and Dictionaries in Data-Analysis Contexts
learning_objective: Create a list to hold a collection of related values and a dictionary to hold one structured record with named fields, then retrieve a value from each using indexing and key access.
description_for_ai: A list holds an ordered collection of values inside square brackets, e.g. daily_sales = [145000, 132000, 45000, 93000], and one item is retrieved by its position starting at 0, e.g. daily_sales[0]. A dictionary holds key-value pairs inside curly braces, e.g. transaction = {"branch": "Lagos", "product": "Rice 50kg"}, and a value is retrieved by its key in square brackets, e.g. transaction["branch"], never by position. A list of dictionaries, one dictionary per record, is exactly the shape of data a spreadsheet row or a pandas DataFrame row takes before it is loaded into a table.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Trying to access a dictionary value using a numeric index like a list, e.g. transaction[0], which raises a KeyError because dictionaries are looked up by key, not position. Misspelling or mis-casing a dictionary key, e.g. transaction["Branch"] when the key is lowercase "branch", which also raises a KeyError since key lookups are case-sensitive. Forgetting that list indexing starts at 0, so asking for the first item as daily_sales[1] actually returns the second item.
example_code_for_ai:
daily_sales = [145000, 132000, 45000, 93000]
transaction = {"branch": "Lagos", "product": "Rice 50kg"}

print(daily_sales[0])
print(transaction["branch"])

title: Conditions and Loops: Applying a Business Rule
learning_objective: Write an if/else statement to apply a threshold rule to one value, then use a for loop to apply that same rule to every value in a list.
description_for_ai: An if statement runs one block of code when a condition is True and, with an else, a different block when it is False, e.g. if sale >= target: ... else: .... A for loop repeats a block of code once for every item in a list, e.g. for sale in daily_sales:, binding the loop variable to each item in turn. Combining a for loop with an if/else inside it applies the same conditional rule to every value in a collection in a single pass, rather than checking each value individually by hand.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Using a single equals sign, sale = target, inside a condition instead of the comparison operator ==, which either raises a SyntaxError or silently reassigns the variable instead of comparing it. Forgetting the colon at the end of the if, else, or for line, which raises a SyntaxError. Misjudging the boundary of a comparison, for example expecting >= 100000 to exclude exactly 100000 when it actually includes it. Forgetting to indent the code inside the loop or if block, which raises an IndentationError.

title: Importing Libraries and Calling Functions
learning_objective: Import a standard library, call one of its functions to perform a calculation, and define a custom function that wraps that calculation for reuse.
description_for_ai: import brings an existing, tested library into a notebook, e.g. import statistics, after which its functions are called as library_name.function_name(...), e.g. statistics.mean(daily_sales). A function is defined with def function_name(parameter): followed by an indented body and a return statement that sends a value back to wherever the function was called. Defining a function does not run it, it must be called separately with parentheses and an argument, e.g. average_sale(daily_sales), to actually execute it and get a result.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Calling a function before the cell that defines it with def has been run, which raises a NameError even though the code looks correct. Writing the function name without parentheses, e.g. average_sale, which returns a reference to the function object itself instead of running it and returning a value. Forgetting the return statement inside a function, so it runs without error but always gives back None instead of the calculated result. Misspelling the imported library's name or one of its functions, e.g. statistic.mean instead of statistics.mean, which raises a NameError or AttributeError.

title: Reading Python Error Messages
learning_objective: Read a Python traceback, identify the error type from its last line, and explain in plain language what that error type means, without needing to fix the code yet.
description_for_ai: A Python traceback reports the error type and message on its final line, which should be read first, e.g. ValueError: could not convert string to float: '₦29,000'. Common error types an analyst meets constantly: NameError means a name was used before being defined or was misspelled; TypeError means an operation was attempted on two incompatible types; ValueError means a value of the right type could not be processed, such as text containing symbols float() cannot interpret; KeyError means a dictionary lookup used a key that does not exist; IndexError means a list was asked for a position beyond its length. Reading the last line first identifies the category of problem before hunting for the specific line that caused it.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reading a traceback top to bottom and stopping at the first unfamiliar-looking line, rather than reading the final line first where the actual error type and message live. Treating every error as the same kind of problem instead of distinguishing what NameError, TypeError, ValueError, KeyError, and IndexError each specifically indicate. Assuming an error means the code is unsalvageable rather than a specific, fixable signal pointing at one exact cause.

title: Debugging a Broken Cell, Step by Step
learning_objective: Locate the exact cause of a broken cell from its error message, apply a single targeted fix, rerun the cell, and verify the corrected result against a value known to be correct.
description_for_ai: Debugging follows a fixed sequence: read the error's last line to identify the cause, locate the exact line and value responsible, change only that one thing, rerun the cell, and check the new result against an independently known correct value rather than assuming it is right because no error appeared. For a ValueError raised by float() on a currency-formatted string, the fix is to remove the offending characters with .replace() before conversion, e.g. value.replace("₦", "").replace(",", ""), chaining two replacements because two different characters need removing.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Changing multiple things in the cell at once when fixing an error, making it unclear which change actually solved the problem. Removing only one of the two problem characters, the currency symbol or the comma, and being surprised the same ValueError still appears. Assuming a cell that now runs without an error must be correct, without checking the output value against anything known independently. Chaining the .replace() calls in a way that targets the wrong variable or the wrong character first.

title: Importing pandas and Loading a CSV
learning_objective: Import pandas using its standard alias and load a CSV file into a DataFrame.
description_for_ai: pandas is imported with the community-standard alias pd, e.g. import pandas as pd, so every later call is written as pd.something instead of pandas.something. pd.read_csv("filename.csv") reads a CSV file from the working directory and returns a DataFrame, pandas' table object, holding every row and column of the file at once. The first row of the CSV becomes the DataFrame's column names automatically unless told otherwise. The result must be assigned to a variable, e.g. df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv"), to be usable in later cells.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing import pandas without the as pd alias, then calling pandas.read_csv(...) later out of habit and getting a NameError because pd was never defined. Forgetting to assign the result of pd.read_csv(...) to a variable, so the DataFrame loads successfully but is immediately lost. Misspelling the file name or omitting the .csv extension, which raises a FileNotFoundError. Assuming a file will load even though it was never uploaded to the current notebook session's storage.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.shape

title: Understanding the DataFrame: Rows, Columns, Index and Values
learning_objective: Identify the rows, columns, index and individual values that make up a DataFrame's structure, given a printed DataFrame.
description_for_ai: A DataFrame is a table: named columns run across the top, exactly like a spreadsheet's header row; an index, a row label, runs down the left, starting at 0 by default; each row is one full record; each individual cell is one value found at the intersection of one row and one column. Printing a DataFrame or calling df.head() displays this structure directly, and the same row-and-column vocabulary used for an Excel worksheet applies unchanged.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming the left-hand index numbers are a column of data rather than row labels pandas generates automatically. Confusing a row, one full transaction, with a column, one field repeated down every transaction. Expecting the index to always start at 1 rather than pandas' default of 0.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.head(3)

title: First Inspection: shape, info, head and tail
learning_objective: Run the standard first-look sequence on a new DataFrame (head, tail, shape, info, describe) and state what each one confirms before trusting the data.
description_for_ai: df.head() and df.tail() show the first or last 5 rows, to sanity-check a load worked and see where a file starts or ends. df.shape returns (rows, columns) as a tuple, confirming size matches expectation. df.info() lists every column with its dtype and non-null count in one view. df.describe() returns summary statistics (count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max) for numeric columns only, ignoring text columns by default.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming df.describe() summarises every column, including text ones like Branch or Product, when by default it only covers numeric columns. Treating df.shape as returning (columns, rows) instead of the actual order, (rows, columns). Skipping this inspection sequence entirely and jumping straight to analysis, then being surprised later by a column with an unexpected type or an unexpectedly small row count.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("future.infer_string", False)
df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
print(df.shape)
df.info()

title: Interpreting Data Types (dtypes)
learning_objective: Read a DataFrame's dtypes and explain why a numeric column with missing values shows as float64 instead of int64.
description_for_ai: df.dtypes lists every column's data type: int64 for whole numbers, float64 for numbers with decimals, object for text (a newer pandas release may label text columns str instead, the taught convention here is object), bool for True/False. A whole-number column that contains even one missing value cannot stay int64, because pandas cannot represent a gap inside a column of pure integers, so the entire column is promoted to float64 to make room for the missing value. This makes dtype itself a diagnostic clue: an unexpectedly float64 column is often a sign of missing data before isna() is even checked.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming a column of whole Naira amounts should always be int64 regardless of whether any values are missing. Treating object and float64 as arbitrary labels rather than as evidence: a text-type column always means text, and an unexpectedly float64 numeric column usually means at least one missing value. Believing dtype is something the analyst sets, rather than something pandas infers automatically from the data on load.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("future.infer_string", False)
df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.dtypes

title: Identifying Missing Values with isna()
learning_objective: Use isna().sum() to count missing values per column and identify exactly which column has gaps before running any calculation.
description_for_ai: df.isna() returns a same-shaped DataFrame of True/False, True wherever a value is missing. Chaining .sum() adds the True values down each column, since True counts as 1 and False as 0, giving one number per column: how many rows are missing a value there. This check belongs before any calculation involving that column, not after a suspicious result appears.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Running isna() alone and trying to read a full grid of True/False values by eye instead of chaining .sum() to get one number per column. Assuming a column with zero missing values reported by isna().sum() cannot have any other kind of data problem, such as an incorrect but present value. Checking for missing values only after a calculation has already produced a strange result, rather than before running it.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.isna().sum()

title: Selecting Columns: Series vs DataFrame
learning_objective: Select a single column as a Series using one set of square brackets, and select multiple columns as a DataFrame using double square brackets, and explain the difference.
description_for_ai: df["Sales"], single brackets and one column name, returns a Series, one labelled column on its own. df[["Sales", "Profit"]], double brackets around a list of names, returns a DataFrame, a smaller table containing just those columns. The two are genuinely different object types, confirmable with type(), not just two different ways of displaying the same thing.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming df["Sales"] and df[["Sales"]] return the same kind of object because they display similarly. Using single brackets with a list of names by mistake, e.g. df["Sales", "Profit"], which raises a KeyError rather than the intended double-bracket selection. Forgetting the second pair of brackets entirely when more than one column is needed.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
print(type(df["Sales"]))
print(type(df[["Sales", "Profit"]]))

title: Filtering Rows with a Boolean Condition
learning_objective: Write a Boolean condition on one column and use it inside square brackets to keep only the matching rows of a DataFrame.
description_for_ai: df["Sales"] > 100000 checks every row and produces a Series of True/False. Wrapping that condition in df[...], e.g. df[df["Sales"] > 100000], keeps only the rows marked True, returning a smaller DataFrame with every original column intact. This is the pandas equivalent of Excel's Filter, applied in one line instead of a dropdown menu.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing the comparison directly on the column name as text instead of the column's values, e.g. "Sales" > 100000, which compares a string to a number and fails, instead of df["Sales"] > 100000. Using a single equals sign instead of a comparison operator inside the filter condition. Forgetting to wrap the whole condition in the outer df[...] and trying to use the True/False Series on its own.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df[df["Sales"] > 100000]

title: Filtering with Multiple Conditions (& and |)
learning_objective: Combine two Boolean conditions on a DataFrame using & for AND and | for OR, with each condition wrapped in its own parentheses.
description_for_ai: & means both conditions must be true; | means either can be true. Each condition needs its own parentheses when combined, e.g. df[(df["Sales"] > 100000) & (df["Region"] == "South West")], because & and | bind tighter than the comparison operators around them, so Python evaluates the wrong part first if the parentheses are left out.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Combining two conditions without parentheses around each one, e.g. df[df["Sales"] > 100000 & df["Region"] == "South West"], which raises a TypeError because & is evaluated before the comparisons complete. Using the plain Python keywords and/or instead of the pandas operators & and |, which raises a ValueError on a Series of more than one value. Using | when the intended logic was & (both required), which returns far more rows than expected.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df[(df["Sales"] > 100000) & (df["Region"] == "South West")]

title: Sorting with sort_values()
learning_objective: Sort a DataFrame by a column in both ascending and descending order, and explain the difference ascending makes.
description_for_ai: df.sort_values("Sales", ascending=False) sorts by the named column, largest to smallest. ascending=True, or omitting the argument entirely since True is the default, sorts smallest to largest instead. sort_values() returns a new sorted DataFrame; it does not change the original in place unless the result is reassigned back to the same variable.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Confusing which direction ascending=True produces, expecting it to put the largest or most important values first when it always means smallest to largest. Calling df.sort_values(...) and expecting df itself to now be sorted, without reassigning the result, e.g. df = df.sort_values(...). Passing the column name as a positional argument in the wrong position relative to ascending.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.sort_values("Sales", ascending=False).head(2)

title: Grouping with groupby()
learning_objective: Group a DataFrame by a category column and aggregate a numeric column within each group, as the pandas equivalent of a PivotTable.
description_for_ai: df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum() follows Group, Select, Aggregate: groupby("Region") groups every row by its Region value, ["Sales"] selects the column to work on inside each group, and .sum() collapses each group to one number. The group labels become the new index, sorted alphabetically by default. This is exactly a PivotTable with Region dragged into Rows and Sales into Values.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Forgetting the aggregation function entirely and expecting df.groupby("Region")["Sales"] alone to produce a usable result, when it is an intermediate grouped object with nothing calculated yet. Grouping by the wrong column relative to the business question being asked, e.g. groupby("Branch") when the question is about Region. Expecting the grouped result's row order to match the order regions first appear in the file, rather than pandas' default alphabetical ordering.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum()

title: Aggregation Functions: sum, mean, count, min, max
learning_objective: Apply sum(), mean(), count(), min() and max() to a column, and state which business question each one answers.
description_for_ai: sum() answers a total-revenue-style question. mean() answers a typical-transaction-size question. count() answers how-many-records question. min() and max() surface the smallest and largest values, each worth checking as a possible data-entry error or a genuine highlight. All five are called the same way, column_name.function_name(), e.g. df["Sales"].mean().
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming mean() and sum() would give the same kind of answer to a business question, when they answer fundamentally different questions, typical size versus total volume. Forgetting the parentheses when calling one of these functions, e.g. df["Sales"].mean, which returns a reference to the method rather than a calculated number. Treating count() as counting something other than non-missing rows in that specific column.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
print(df["Sales"].sum(), df["Sales"].mean(), df["Sales"].count())

title: Multiple Aggregations at Once with .agg()
learning_objective: Use .agg() with a list of function names to calculate several aggregations on one grouped column in a single call.
description_for_ai: df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"]) runs all three aggregations at once and returns one table with a column per aggregation, rather than three separate groupby lines run individually. Function names inside .agg() are passed as strings in a list, matching the pandas method names exactly, e.g. "sum" not sum.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Passing the function names as bare identifiers instead of strings inside the list, e.g. [sum, mean] confused with Python's built-in sum instead of "sum" as pandas expects. Running three separate groupby lines when one .agg() call would give the same answer with one line and one easily comparable table. Expecting .agg() to change the underlying DataFrame rather than returning a new summary table.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])

title: Creating and Verifying Calculated Columns
learning_objective: Create a new column from an arithmetic expression on existing columns, and verify it against a figure already recorded in the source data.
description_for_ai: df["Profit_check"] = df["Sales"] - df["Cost"] creates a brand new column, applying the calculation to every row at once. Verification compares the new column to an existing one the source system already recorded, e.g. (df["Profit_check"] == df["Profit"]).all(), which returns a single True only if every row matches exactly, confirming the calculation and the source data agree rather than assuming it.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Using a single equals sign inside the comparison meant for verification, e.g. df["Profit_check"] = df["Profit"] instead of ==, which overwrites the column instead of comparing it. Checking only the first few rows by eye instead of using .all() to confirm every row matches. Assuming a calculated column is correct simply because it ran without an error, rather than checking it against an independently known value.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df["Profit_check"] = df["Sales"] - df["Cost"]
(df["Profit_check"] == df["Profit"]).all()

title: NumPy Conditional Calculations
learning_objective: Use np.where() to create a column that assigns one of two values based on a condition, applied to every row of a DataFrame at once.
description_for_ai: NumPy is the numerical engine pandas is built on; every pandas column is a NumPy array underneath, which is why dtypes are named int64 and float64, NumPy's own names. np.where(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) checks a condition across every row and returns the first value where it is True and the second where it is False, e.g. df["Sales_Tier"] = np.where(df["Sales"] > 100000, "High", "Low"). np.round(numbers, decimals) rounds a numeric column or calculation to a set number of decimal places.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Forgetting import numpy as np before calling np.where(), which raises a NameError. Supplying the two outcome values in the wrong order, swapping what should happen when the condition is True versus False. Expecting np.where() on a column containing a missing value to produce a sensible result for that row, when a NaN input still produces a NaN or unexpected output rather than a clean True/False branch.
example_code_for_ai:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df["Sales_Tier"] = np.where(df["Sales"] > 100000, "High", "Low")
df["Sales_Tier"].value_counts()

title: Reproducing an Excel Analysis in pandas
learning_objective: Reproduce a PivotTable-style analysis (grouped total and average) in pandas, and confirm the result matches what Excel would have produced.
description_for_ai: A PivotTable with a category in Rows and two value fields (a sum and an average) translates directly into one pandas call combining groupby() and .agg() with named results, e.g. df.groupby("Region").agg(Total_Sales=("Sales", "sum"), Avg_Margin=("Margin_%", "mean")).sort_values("Total_Sales", ascending=False). Matching Excel's own numbers exactly is the verification step, not an assumption that the pandas code is automatically correct because it runs.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming a pandas result that looks reasonable must match Excel without actually comparing the two figure for figure. Naming the aggregated columns inside .agg() inconsistently with what is referenced afterwards in .sort_values(), causing a KeyError. Treating this reproduction step as optional once the pandas code runs, rather than as the actual point of the exercise: proving pandas and Excel agree.
example_code_for_ai:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Optimum_branch_sales.csv")
df["Margin_%"] = (df["Profit"] / df["Sales"] * 100).round(1)
df.groupby("Region").agg(
    Total_Sales=("Sales", "sum"),
    Avg_Margin=("Margin_%", "mean"),
).sort_values("Total_Sales", ascending=False)

title: Writing Strong AI Prompts for pandas Code
learning_objective: Write a prompt for an AI assistant that includes dataset structure, column names, the analytical objective and the expected output, and explain why each element improves the result.
description_for_ai: A weak prompt such as "write pandas code" gives an AI assistant no dataset, no columns and no defined goal, so it has to guess. A strong prompt states the DataFrame's variable name and column names, the exact analytical question, and what the output should look like, e.g. naming that df has columns Region and Margin_%, and asking for the average Margin_% per Region sorted highest to lowest. Each of these details removes one guess the assistant would otherwise have to make.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing a prompt with the analytical goal but no column names, forcing the assistant to guess plausible-sounding names that may not match the real DataFrame. Assuming a vague prompt and a specific prompt are equally likely to produce correct code, when the specific one removes the exact assumptions that lead to wrong column names or wrong logic. Treating prompt-writing as optional once you already know pandas, rather than as a skill in its own right.
example_code_for_ai:
# Weak prompt: "Write pandas code."

# Strong prompt:
# "I have a pandas DataFrame called df with a column Margin_%
# already calculated as Profit divided by Sales times 100.
# Write code to show the average Margin_% for each Region,
# sorted from highest to lowest."

title: Asking AI to Explain Code, and Verifying the Explanation
learning_objective: Ask an AI assistant to explain a piece of pandas code line by line, then check that explanation against what the code is already known to do.
description_for_ai: Asking an assistant to "explain this code line by line, as if I am a beginner data analyst" produces a plain-language walkthrough of what each line does. That explanation is itself AI output and needs the same scrutiny as generated code: check it against the actual result the code produced, or against what the trainee already expects the code to do, rather than trusting it purely because it sounds confident and coherent.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting an AI explanation of code at face value simply because it is fluent and confident, without checking it against the real output. Assuming that being able to follow an explanation is the same thing as being able to reproduce or defend the code independently. Skipping this step entirely for code that already appears to run without error.
example_code_for_ai:
# code being explained:
# df.groupby("Region")["Margin_%"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
#
# prompt: "Explain this pandas code line by line, as if I am
# a beginner data analyst."

title: Debugging AI-Generated Code with Full Error Context
learning_objective: Fix an AI-suggested pandas method that no longer exists, by pasting the full error message and the exact code back to the assistant rather than a vague description.
description_for_ai: df.sort("Cost", ascending=False) raises AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'sort', because sort() was removed from pandas some years ago in favour of sort_values(). Effective AI-assisted debugging pastes the complete error message and the exact failing code back to the assistant along with the intended goal, rather than a vague report like "it doesn't work", which gives the assistant nothing concrete to diagnose.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reporting only "it doesn't work" to an AI assistant instead of pasting the full traceback and the exact code that produced it. Assuming an AI-suggested method name is correct simply because it sounds plausible for the task, without checking it actually exists on the object being called. Applying an AI's suggested fix without rerunning the corrected code to confirm the error is actually resolved.
example_code_for_ai:
df.sort("Cost", ascending=False)
# Raises: AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'sort'

# Fixed:
df.sort_values("Cost", ascending=False)

title: Identifying AI Hallucinations and Logically Incorrect Code
learning_objective: Identify an AI-generated calculation that runs without any error but produces a logically impossible result, and state which check would catch it.
description_for_ai: AI-generated code can be syntactically valid, reference real columns, and run without raising any error while still being wrong, for example calculating an average margin with .sum() instead of .mean(), e.g. df["Margin_%"].sum() giving 300.0 when every individual transaction's margin is 15.0%. An average per-transaction percentage above 100% is not possible, so the checklist question "does the output make sense" catches this even though the code never threw an error.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming that code which runs without an error must therefore be logically correct. Not sanity-checking a result against a plausible real-world range, such as recognising that an average percentage margin over 100% cannot be right. Treating an AI hallucination as something that always produces a visible error, rather than sometimes producing a confident, wrong number instead.
example_code_for_ai:
df["Margin_%"].sum()    # 300.0, wrong: sums instead of averaging
df["Margin_%"].mean()   # 15.0, correct

title: The Verification Checklist Before Trusting AI Code
learning_objective: Apply a six-question verification checklist to any AI-generated pandas code before accepting its result: does it run, does it use the correct columns, does the output make sense, does it answer the original question, can the result be reproduced another way, and can every line be explained.
description_for_ai: Before AI-generated code is trusted, six questions get checked in order: does the code run; does it use the correct, real column names; does the output make sense as a plausible number; does the result actually answer the original business question that was asked; can the same result be reproduced a different way as a cross-check; and can every line be explained without help. All six apply every time, regardless of how confident or fluent the AI's response looked.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating "the code ran without an error" as sufficient on its own, skipping the remaining five checklist questions. Checking whether the output makes sense in isolation, without also confirming it actually answers the specific business question that was originally asked. Applying the checklist inconsistently, for short or simple-looking snippets but not for longer ones.
example_code_for_ai:
# the checklist, applied to any AI-generated snippet:
# 1. Does it run?
# 2. Does it use the correct columns?
# 3. Does the output make sense?
# 4. Does it answer the original question?
# 5. Can I reproduce it another way?
# 6. Can I explain every line?

title: The "Explain It Back" Rule
learning_objective: State and apply the rule that code cannot be submitted unless the person submitting it can explain every line of it without assistance.
description_for_ai: The rule is: if you cannot explain the code, you cannot submit the code. In a paired activity, one partner explains a line of AI-assisted code out loud while the other asks questions about anything unclear, then the two swap roles on a different line. Any single line that neither partner can explain must be investigated and understood before it goes anywhere near a submission, regardless of how correct the final number appears to be.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating a correct final output as proof that every line leading to it is understood. Allowing one line in a longer snippet to go unexplained because the overall result looked right. Rehearsing an explanation from memory without genuinely understanding it, which becomes apparent the moment a partner asks a follow-up question.
example_code_for_ai:
# Paired activity structure:
# Partner A explains one line out loud.
# Partner B asks a question about anything unclear.
# Swap roles, repeat on a different line.
# Any unexplained line is investigated before submission.
